claim: Both visual and auditory spatial selective attention result in lateralized alpha (8–14 Hz) oscillatory power in parietal cortex, with alpha increasing in the hemisphere ipsilateral to attentional focus.
source: Both visual and auditory spatial selective attention result in lateralized alpha (8–14 Hz) oscillatory power in parietal cortex: alpha increases in the hemisphere ipsilateral to attentional focus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is consistent with established findings in the field.

claim: Brain stimulation studies suggest a causal relationship between parietal alpha and suppression of the representation of contralateral visual space.
source: Brain stimulation studies suggest a causal relationship between parietal alpha and suppression of the representation of contralateral visual space.
evidence: This claim is based on references to prior brain stimulation studies.

claim: There is no evidence that parietal alpha controls auditory spatial attention prior to this study.
source: However, there is no evidence that parietal alpha controls auditory spatial attention.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior evidence, based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Alpha (10 Hz) but not theta (6 Hz) HD-tACS of right parietal cortex interfered with attending left but not right auditory space.
source: Alpha (10 Hz) but not theta (6 Hz) HD-tACS of right parietal cortex interfered with attending left but not right auditory space.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Parietal stimulation had no effect for nonspatial auditory attention.
source: Parietal stimulation had no effect for nonspatial auditory attention.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Performance in post-stimulation trials returned rapidly to baseline.
source: Moreover, performance in post-stimulation trials returned rapidly to baseline.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no persistent effects after stimulation ended.

claim: The results demonstrate a causal, frequency-, hemispheric-, and task-specific effect of parietal alpha brain stimulation on top-down control of auditory spatial attention.
source: These results demonstrate a causal, frequency-, hemispheric-, and task-specific effect of parietal alpha brain stimulation on top-down control of auditory spatial attention.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data and multiple control conditions.

claim: Parietal cortex interacts with frontal cortex to control spatial attention in both vision and audition.
source: Parietal cortex interacts with frontal cortex to control spatial attention in both vision and audition (Farah et al., 1989; Green et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) reveals a series of retinotopically mapped regions ascending along the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), which are biased towards representing contralateral exocentric space.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) reveals a series of retinotopically mapped regions ascending along the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), which are biased towards representing contralateral exocentric space (Sereno et al., 2001; Swisher et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Earlier mapped regions in the IPS are strongly engaged only by vision, while higher maps are recruited when participants engage spatial auditory attention.
source: While the earlier mapped regions are strongly engaged only by vision, the higher maps are recruited when participants engage spatial auditory attention (Michalka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Alpha oscillations (8–14 Hz) are associated with a range of neural functions.
source: Alpha oscillations (8–14 Hz) are associated with a range of neural functions (Klimesch, 2012; Weisz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Parietal cortex generates strong alpha oscillations measurable using electro- and magneto-encephalography (EEG and MEG).
source: Parietal cortex generates strong alpha oscillations measurable using electro- and magneto-encephalography (EEG and MEG) (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Kelly et al., 2006; Worden et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When listeners focus visual attention, alpha power lateralizes, increasing in the parietal hemisphere ipsilateral to the direction of attention and decreasing contralaterally.
source: When listeners focus visual attention, alpha power lateralizes, increasing in the parietal hemisphere ipsilateral to the direction of attention and decreasing contralaterally (Kelly et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Auditory spatial attention results in lateralized parietal alpha activity.
source: Auditory spatial attention also results in lateralized parietal alpha activity (Banerjee et al., 2011; Mehraei et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019; Wöstmann et al., 2016; Frey et al., 2014; Strauß et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Alpha lateralization shifts systematically as the focus of auditory spatial attention shifts from far-left to far-right.
source: indeed, alpha lateralization shifts systematically as the focus of auditory spatial attention shifts from far-left to far-right (Mehraei et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2020) (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1A showing this pattern.

claim: Focusing spatial attention in both vision and audition leads to similar parietal alpha activity.
source: These results suggest that focusing spatial attention in both vision and audition leads to similar parietal alpha activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research on alpha lateralization in both modalities.

claim: Auditory spatial processing relies on retinotopic regions of parietal cortex, but processing nonspatial features does not, even when listeners are attending the same source in the same sound mixture.
source: While auditory spatial processing relies on retinotopic regions of parietal cortex, processing nonspatial features does not, even when listeners are attending the same source in the same sound mixture (Michalka et al., 2016; Hill and Miller, 2010; Noyce et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For a target defined by its location, alpha lateralization appears only transiently at the start of a trial if competing streams have distinct nonspatial features.
source: Indeed, for a target defined by its location, alpha lateralization appears only transiently at the start of a trial if competing streams have distinct nonspatial features (Bonacci et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Spatial auditory attention utilizes parietal cortex and produces lateralized alpha.
source: Thus, spatial auditory attention utilizes parietal cortex and produces lateralized alpha
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research on parietal involvement and alpha lateralization during spatial attention.

claim: Nonspatial auditory attention does not utilize parietal cortex and produces no signature of attentional focus in parietal cortex.
source: however, nonspatial auditory attention does not and produces no signature of attentional focus in parietal cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research showing lack of parietal involvement in nonspatial attention.

claim: Maintaining attention on an ongoing auditory stream is supported by continuity of features like pitch, location, voice, and timbre.
source: Numerous behavioral studies demonstrate that maintaining attention on an ongoing auditory stream is supported by continuity of features like pitch, location, voice, and timbre (Best et al., 2008; Darwin and Carlyon, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Feature continuity influences performance automatically: even when listeners know they should ignore some feature, discontinuities in the task-irrelevant feature disrupt attention.
source: Feature continuity influences performance automatically: even when listeners know they should ignore some feature, such as talker identity, and attend to a different feature, such as location, discontinuities in the task-irrelevant feature disrupt attention (Best et al., 2008; Maddox and Shinn-Cunningham, 2012; Bressler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Effects of talker continuity on speech perception in quiet have been ascribed to 'talker normalization,' but may actually be due to disruptions of attention triggered by a talker change.
source: Indeed, effects of talker continuity on speech perception in quiet have been ascribed to 'talker normalization,' but may actually be due to disruptions of attention triggered by a talker change (Lim et al., 2019; Choi and Perrachione, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research reinterpreting prior findings.

claim: Talker discontinuity during an auditory spatial attention task interferes with recall of the target stream and disrupts parietal alpha lateralization.
source: Talker discontinuity during an auditory spatial attention task not only interferes with recall of the target stream, it disrupts parietal alpha lateralization (Mehraei et al., 2018) (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and reference to Figure 1B showing this effect.

claim: In switching trials when listeners were instructed to listen to syllables from one direction (ignoring any talker change), errors were elevated for the syllable right after the talker switch and subsequent alpha lateralization was disrupted.
source: In switching trials when listeners were instructed to listen to syllables from one direction (ignoring any talker change), errors were elevated for the syllable right after the talker switch —and subsequent alpha lateralization was disrupted (see bottom of Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Mehraei et al., 2018) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Talker continuity overrides top-down, volitional control of spatial attention; when the talker from the attended location jumps to the opposite side of the listener, the talker discontinuity interrupts spatial attention and parietal alpha lateralization.
source: These results suggest that talker continuity overrides top-down, volitional control of spatial attention; when the talker from the attended location jumps to the opposite side of the listener, the talker discontinuity interrupts spatial attention and parietal alpha lateralization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of Mehraei et al. (2018).

claim: TMS inactivation of parietal cortex in one hemisphere causes spatially specific visual processing changes, enhancing spatial attention directed ipsilaterally but degrading it contralaterally.
source: TMS inactivation of parietal cortex in one hemisphere causes spatially specific visual processing changes, enhancing spatial attention directed ipsilaterally but degrading it contralaterally (Hilgetag et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior TMS research.

claim: Unilateral TMS inactivation of the frontal eye field (FEF) reduces alpha coupling between prefrontal and parietal cortices; moreover, parietal alpha lateralization is disrupted and this disruption predicts increases in reaction times during a visual working memory task.
source: Unilateral TMS inactivation of the frontal eye field (FEF, part of the fronto-parietal visuo-spatial attention network) reduces alpha coupling between prefrontal and parietal cortices; moreover, parietal alpha lateralization is disrupted and this disruption predicts increases in reaction times during a visual working memory task (Sauseng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior TMS research.

claim: Unilateral 20 Hz rTMS (which disrupts alpha oscillations) of either FEF or parietal cortex has similar effects on alpha coupling and lateralization.
source: Unilateral 20 Hz rTMS (which disrupts alpha oscillations) of either FEF or parietal cortex has similar effects (Capotosto et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior rTMS research.

claim: Alpha-rate rTMS of parietal cortex enhances performance for ipsilateral targets and degrades performance for contralateral targets for visual spatial attention and working memory tasks, while stimulation at non-alpha frequencies has no effect.
source: Alpha-rate rTMS of parietal cortex enhances performance for ipsilateral targets and degrades performance for contralateral targets for visual spatial attention (Romei et al., 2010) and working memory (Sauseng et al., 2009) tasks, while stimulation at non-alpha frequencies has no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior rTMS research.

claim: Two studies failed to find frequency- or retinotopically specific effects of parietal tACS stimulation on visual tasks.
source: Two studies failed to find frequency- or retinotopically specific effects of parietal tACS stimulation on visual tasks (Brignani et al., 2013; Veniero et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior tACS research.

claim: A high-density tACS (HD-tACS) study found that parietal alpha stimulation affects volitional control of visual spatial attention, improving performance for targets ipsilateral to the stimulation.
source: while a high-density tACS (HD-tACS) found that parietal alpha stimulation affects volitional control of visual spatial attention, improving performance for targets ipsilateral to the stimulation (Schuhmann, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior HD-tACS research.

claim: Stimulation of auditory cortex can influence auditory task performance, including spatially specific effects on auditory selective attention.
source: A few studies have shown that stimulation of auditory cortex can influence auditory task performance (Riecke et al., 2018; Riecke et al., 2015; Zoefel et al., 2018; Neuling et al., 2012), including spatially specific effects on auditory selective attention (Wöstmann et al., 2018; Hanenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on auditory cortex stimulation.

claim: HD-tACS uses an electrode ring configuration (e.g., an anode flanked by multiple cathodes) and creates a more focused electrical current sink compared to traditional tACS.
source: Compared to traditional tACS (conducted through sponge pads), HD-tACS, which uses an electrode ring configuration (e.g., an anode flanked by multiple cathodes), creates a more focused electrical current sink (Kuo et al., 2013; Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on HD-tACS methodology.

claim: HD-tACS allows for more precise anatomical targeting than traditional tACS.
source: This allows for more precise anatomical targeting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the more focused current sink produced by HD-tACS.

claim: Combined with improved computational models of predicted current flow in the brain, HD-tACS yields more precise brain stimulation than traditional approaches.
source: Combined with improved computational models of predicted current flow in the brain (Datta et al., 2009; Edwards et al., 2013), HD-tACS yields more precise brain stimulation than traditional approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on computational modeling and is an inference about the combined benefits.

claim: The study targeted right intraparietal sulcus (rIPS) based on previous findings suggesting that right parietal cortex contains the only representation of left exocentric space, whereas right space is represented strongly in left IPS but also weakly in rIPS.
source: We targeted right intraparietal sulcus (rIPS) based on previous findings suggesting that right parietal cortex contains the only representation of left exocentric space, whereas right space is represented strongly in left IPS but also weakly in rIPS (Farah et al., 1989; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2011; Shulman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on hemispheric asymmetry in spatial representation.

claim: During spatial attention, rIPS alpha stimulation was expected to suppress the representation of left exocentric space, impairing performance for leftward targets.
source: During spatial attention, we expected rIPS alpha stimulation to suppress the representation of left exocentric space, impairing performance for leftward targets (see Figure 3, bottom left panel).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, based on prior knowledge and depicted in Figure 3.

claim: Performance for rightward targets was hypothesized to either be unchanged (as rIPS should already have strong alpha due to top-down spatial attention) or enhanced (if stimulation led to even better suppression of the leftward distractor).
source: We had a secondary hypothesis that performance for rightward targets might either be unchanged (as rIPS should already have strong alpha due to top-down spatial attention) or enhanced (if stimulation led to even better suppression of the leftward distractor; see Figure 3, bottom right panel).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, based on reasoning about alpha dynamics and depicted in Figure 3.

claim: When listeners attended to the left, performance changed in the expected direction, dropping from 87.40% correct in continuous trials to 65.29% in switching trials in the main experiment.
source: When listeners attended to the left, performance changed in the expected direction, dropping from 87.40% correct in continuous trials to 65.29% in switching trials (Z(19) = 3.91, Padj <0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: When listeners attended to the right, performance dropped from 88.27% for continuous to 64.81% for switching trials in the main experiment.
source: When listeners attended to the right, performance also dropped, from 88.27% for continuous to 64.81% for switching trials (Z(19) = 3.90, Padj <0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: When listeners directed attention to a specific talker in the main experiment, the average accuracy dropped slightly for switching compared to continuous trials for both attend-female (79.62% to 79.13%) and attend-male (85.48% to 81.44%) trials.
source: When listeners directed attention to a specific talker, the average accuracy also dropped slightly for switching compared to continuous trials for both attend-female (79.62% to 79.13%) and attend-male (85.48% to 81.44%) trials.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: For attend-female trials in the main experiment, the change from continuous to switching was not significant (Z(19) = 0.20, Padj >0.99).
source: For attend-female trials, this change was not significant (Z(19) = 0.20, Padj >0.99)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: For attend-male trials in the main experiment, the change from continuous to switching reached significance (Z(19) = 2.36, Padj = 0.036).
source: however, it did reach significance for attend-male trials (Z(19) = 2.36, Padj = 0.036).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: In the control experiment, when listeners attended to the left, performance dropped from 79.81% correct in continuous trials to 56.84% correct in the switching trials.
source: When listeners attended to the left, performance dropped as expected, from 79.81% correct in continuous trials to 56.84% correct in the switching trials (Z(17) = 3.66, Padj <0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment data with statistical support.

claim: In the control experiment, when listeners attended to the right, performance dropped from 80.77% to 57.26%.
source: When listeners attended to the right, performance dropped from 80.77% to 57.26% (Z(17) = 3.71, Padj <0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment data with statistical support.

claim: In the control experiment, when listeners directed attention to a specific talker, average accuracy was lower for switching than continuous trials for both attend-female (77.35% to 70.51%) and attend-male (74.79% to 70.62%) trials.
source: When listeners directed attention to a specific talker, average accuracy was lower for switching than continuous trials for both attend-female (77.35% to 70.51%) and attend-male (74.79% to 70.62%) trials.
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment data.

claim: In the control experiment, the change from continuous to switching reached statistical significance for the attend-female trials (Z(17) = 2.76, Padj = 0.011), but not the attend-male trials (Z(17) = 1.86, Padj = 0.13).
source: This change reached statistical significance for the attend-female trials (Z(17) = 2.76, Padj = 0.011), but not the attend-male trials (Z(17) = 1.86, Padj = 0.13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control experiment data.

claim: The study found a larger drop in performance from continuous to switching trials than in Mehraei et al. (2018), consistent with the fact that talkers switched after each syllable in the current study, which should be more disruptive than a single switch.
source: It is worth noting that our talkers switched after each syllable (see Figure 2B), which should be more disruptive than a single switch (as in Mehraei et al., 2018, which inspired this manipulation). Consistent with this, we found a larger drop in performance from continuous to switching trials than in Mehraei et al. (2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current study's design and results with prior research.

claim: There was no significant difference in baseline performance between Sham and Stimulation sessions in either the main experiment (Z(19) = 0.068, p=0.95) or the control experiment (Z(17) = 0.46, p=0.65).
source: We first confirmed that there was no significant difference in baseline performance between Sham and Stimulation sessions in either the main experiment (Z(19) = 0.068, p=0.95, Wilcoxon rank test) or the control experiment (Z(17) = 0.46, p=0.65, Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Counter-balancing the session order canceled out any systematic effects of testing order.
source: Thus, counter-balancing the session order canceled out any systematic effects of testing order.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant difference in baseline performance between sessions.

claim: Individual subjects' performance across sessions was significantly correlated in both the main experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.48; p=0.032) and the control experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.52; p=0.028), indicating the stability of individual differences across testing days.
source: We found that individual subjects' performance across sessions was significantly correlated in both the main experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.48; p=0.032) and the control experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.52; p=0.028), indicating the stability of individual differences across testing days.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, with an inference about what it indicates.

claim: For rIPS alpha stimulation, performance in the 'stimulation' block was significantly worse in the Stimulation session than in the Sham session for left attention (Z(19) = 2.10, Padj = 0.036).
source: Specifically, for rIPS alpha stimulation, performance in the 'stimulation' block was significantly worse in the Stimulation session than in the Sham session for left attention (Z(19) = 2.10, Padj = 0.036, Wilcoxon signed rank test, corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: There was no significant increase in performance from Sham to Stimulation sessions for right attention (Z(19) = 1.27, Padj > 0.99).
source: There was no significant increase in performance from Sham to Stimulation sessions for right attention (Z(19) = 1.27, Padj > 0.99; see Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Baseline-corrected performance was consistently lower in the Stimulation session compared to the Sham session for each of the sub-blocks in the 'stimulation' block.
source: We observed a consistent, sustained effect of stimulation: baseline-corrected performance was lower in the Stimulation session compared to the Sham session for each of the sub-blocks in the 'stimulation' block (left side of Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from post hoc analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The difference in performance between Stimulation and Sham sessions disappeared by the first post-stimulation sub-block, immediately after HD-tACS stopped.
source: This difference disappeared by the first post-stimulation sub-block, immediately after HD-tACS stopped; baseline-corrected performance was indistinguishable for the Sham and Stimulation sessions for the final four sub-blocks (right side of Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from post hoc analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Of the 32 distinct trial types, Sham vs. Stimulation sessions differed significantly only in one, in the expected direction: during alpha stimulation of rIPS, when listeners directed spatial attention to a continuous-talker target that was on the left.
source: Of the 32 distinct trial types, Sham vs. Stimulation sessions differed significantly only in one, in the expected direction: during alpha stimulation of rIPS, when listeners directed spatial attention to a continuous-talker target that was on the left (top leftmost panel in Figure 7A, repeated from Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical analyses across all conditions, referencing Figure 7A.

claim: There was no effect of theta stimulation for any of the 16 trial types in the control experiment: for all of these, Z(17) < 1.67 (p>0.095).
source: In addition, there was no effect of theta stimulation for any of the 16 trial types in the control experiment [(spatial and nonspatial attention) x (during stimulation and post stimulation) x (continuous trials and switching trials) x (left/female and right/male)]: for all of these, Z(17) < 1.67 (p>0.095).
evidence: This is a summary of statistical results from the control experiment.

claim: Comparing baseline-corrected performance for Sham vs. Stimulation sessions during nonspatial attention, there was no effect of stimulation for targets from either the left (Z(19) = 0.23, p=0.82) or the right (Z(19) = 1.30, p=0.19).
source: Comparing baseline-corrected performance for Sham vs. Stimulation sessions during nonspatial attention, we observed no effect of stimulation for targets from either the left (Z(19) = 0.23, p=0.82) or the right (Z(19) = 1.30, p=0.19).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The lack of effect of parietal stimulation on nonspatial attention trials (even when analyzed by target location) further supports the view that alpha stimulation of parietal cortex only influences top-down spatial processing.
source: These results further support the view that alpha stimulation of parietal cortex only influences top-down spatial processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of stimulation effects during nonspatial attention.

claim: The study shows a causal relationship between parietal alpha power and spatial auditory attention using HD-tACS to stimulate rIPS.
source: Using HD-tACS to stimulate rIPS, we here show a causal relationship between parietal alpha power and spatial auditory attention.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Right HD-tACS parietal stimulation disrupted selective attention directed to the left.
source: We found that right HD-tACS parietal stimulation disrupted selective attention directed to the left.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: There was no effect of parietal stimulation on performance when listeners focused top-down attention based on talker identity, when the talker in the attended direction switched abruptly, or when theta stimulation was employed.
source: We found no effect on performance in the myriad control conditions (i.e., when listeners focused top-down attention based on talker identity, when the talker in the attended direction switched abruptly, or when theta stimulation was employed).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the control conditions in the experimental data.

claim: Alpha HD-tACS stimulation produced an effect size of 0.33 for leftward spatial attention, which is comparable to those in past published reports of tACS effects on cognitive function in healthy adults (Ē=0.36, 95% CI = 0.27–0.46) as well as tDCS studies (e.g., Ē = 0.23, 95% CI = 0.09–0.36).
source: In our study, alpha HD-tACS stimulation produced an effect size of 0.33 for leftward spatial attention. A meta-analysis study (Schutter and Wischnewski, 2016) shows that this effect size is comparable to those in past published reports of tACS effects on cognitive function in healthy adults (Ē=0.36, 95% CI = 0.27–0.46) as well as tDCS studies (e.g., Ē = 0.23, 95% CI = 0.09–0.36) (Brunoni and Vanderhasselt, 2014; Hill et al., 2016; Klaus and Schutter, 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's effect size with those reported in prior meta-analyses.

claim: The frequency specificity of HD-tACS parietal stimulation (alpha but not theta) implicates alpha in control of auditory spatial attention.
source: This frequency specificity of HD-tACS parietal stimulation implicates alpha in control of auditory spatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of alpha vs. theta stimulation.

claim: The spatial specificity of the effect of rIPS stimulation (affecting left but not right attention) is consistent with the hypothesis that parietal alpha causally suppresses the representation of contralateral space, steering spatial attention.
source: Regardless, the spatial specificity of the effect of rIPS stimulation is consistent with the hypothesis that parietal alpha causally suppresses the representation of contralateral space, steering spatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial specificity of the stimulation effects.

claim: Previous visual attention studies show that alpha-tACS increases endogenous alpha oscillations only when alpha power is low.
source: First, previous visual attention studies show that alpha-tACS increases endogenous alpha oscillations only when alpha power is low (Alagapan et al., 2016; Neuling et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Top-down attention to the right should naturally produce strong rIPS alpha, limiting the influence of additional alpha power.
source: Top-down attention to the right should naturally produce strong rIPS alpha, limiting the influence of additional alpha power (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge about alpha lateralization during spatial attention, depicted in Figure 3.

claim: Intrinsic rIPS alpha power should be low during leftward attention, allowing stimulation to have an observable effect.
source: In contrast, intrinsic rIPS alpha power should be low during leftward attention, allowing stimulation to have an observable effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge about alpha lateralization during spatial attention.

claim: Parietal cortex is asymmetrical; rIPS predominantly represents left space, but also has a weak representation of right space.
source: Second, parietal cortex is asymmetrical; rIPS predominantly represents left space, but also has a weak representation of right space.
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge about hemispheric asymmetry in spatial representation.

claim: When listeners attended to the right, an injection of alpha energy to rIPS may have enhanced suppression of the dominant leftward distractor, but it may also have spread to suppress the weak representation of the rightward target, leading to little net change.
source: When listeners attended to the right, an injection of alpha energy to rIPS may have enhanced suppression of the dominant leftward distractor, but it may also have spread to suppress the weak representation of the rightward target, leading to little net change.
evidence: This is speculation about why no effect was observed for rightward attention.

claim: The results implicate parietal alpha in volitional steering of auditory spatial attention.
source: Thus, our results implicate parietal alpha in volitional steering of auditory spatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the task-specificity and stimulus-specificity of the stimulation effects.

claim: Schumann and colleagues found that parietal alpha stimulation caused a spatially specific effect in an endogenous attention task, decreasing reaction times for ipsilateral targets, but had no impact on exogenous attention or simple detection tasks.
source: In this case, and only this case, parietal alpha stimulation caused a spatially specific effect, decreasing reaction times for ipsilateral targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schuhmann, 2019).

claim: While parietal alpha modulates volitional control of spatial attention tasks, it does not robustly influence exogenous attention.
source: These findings highlight the importance of carefully considering task demands when interpreting results of parietal stimulation studies. While parietal alpha modulates volitional control of spatial attention tasks, it does not robustly influence exogenous attention.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results across multiple studies, including Schuhmann (2019).

claim: The sudden appearance of a new stimulus, even one near threshold, may draw exogenous attention, which may override any effects of parietal processing and render alpha parietal stimulation impotent.
source: The sudden appearance of a new stimulus, even one near threshold, may draw exogenous attention (Desimone and Duncan, 1995), which may override any effects of parietal processing and render alpha parietal stimulation impotent (Brignani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about why some studies failed to find effects of parietal stimulation, supported by citations.

claim: Traditional tACS is usually delivered with large pads (5 × 5 cm2) and stimulates a broad area between the stimulation electrodes.
source: Traditional tACS is usually delivered with large pads (5 × 5 cm2) and stimulates a broad area between the stimulation electrodes (Datta et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on tACS methodology.

claim: The spread of electric current with traditional tACS is greater than with HD-tACS, and could even spread to both hemispheres, confounding stimulation effects.
source: The resulting spread of electric current is greater, and could even spread to both hemispheres, confounding stimulation effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of traditional tACS.

claim: The current study's HD-tACS stimulation targeted intraparietal sulcus and produces essentially no current in auditory sensory regions.
source: In contrast to their study, our HD-tACS stimulation targeted intraparietal sulcus and produces essentially no current in auditory sensory regions (see Figure 8C).
evidence: This is based on the current flow modeling shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The current study demonstrates that alpha in IPS, which is a part of the well-studied visuo-spatial attention network, plays a causal role in spatial auditory attention.
source: However, ours demonstrates that alpha in IPS, which is a part of the well-studied visuo-spatial attention network, plays a causal role in spatial auditory attention
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and the targeted stimulation location.

claim: By including a nonspatial attention task as a control, the study shows that the influence of IPS alpha depends specifically on top-down engagement of the visuo-spatial attention network.
source: By including a nonspatial attention task as a control, our study further shows that the influence of IPS alpha depends specifically on top-down engagement of the visuo-spatial attention network; there is no influence of IPS alpha stimulation when listeners attend to the same auditory source within the same physical sound mixture using nonspatial auditory features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of stimulation effects during nonspatial attention.

claim: Auditory spatial attention recruits the same fronto-parietal network involved in visual spatial attention.
source: We believe that auditory spatial attention recruits the same fronto-parietal network involved in visual spatial attention (Michalka et al., 2016; see the discussion in Bonacci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a belief/hypothesis of the authors, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Manipulation of parietal alpha is expected to lead to similar effects for auditory spatial attention and visual spatial attention.
source: We therefore expect manipulation of parietal alpha to lead to similar effects for auditory spatial attention and visual spatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hypothesis that auditory and visual spatial attention use the same network.

claim: The current study found that manipulation of parietal alpha affects control of endogenous spatial attention (processing of continuous contralateral targets during a spatial attention task) but does not influence performance dominated by exogenous attention effects (processing of switching targets).
source: As in Schuhmann (2019), we found that manipulation of parietal alpha affects control of endogenous spatial attention (processing of continuous contralateral targets during a spatial attention task)—but does not influence performance dominated by exogenous attention effects (processing of switching targets, where endogenous disruptions limit performance).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings, drawing a parallel to Schuhmann (2019).

claim: Even with HD-tACS, the induced current intensity is not uniformly distributed throughout rIPS.
source: However, even with this approach, the induced current intensity is not uniformly distributed throughout rIPS (see Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on the current flow modeling shown in Figure 8.

claim: IPS is both narrow and relatively long.
source: IPS is both narrow and relatively long.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The current-flow estimate of the stimulation suggests the strongest stimulation arises in the most posterior regions of IPS (IPS1 and IPS24); however, auditory spatial attention relies primarily on higher IPS regions.
source: The current-flow estimate of the stimulation we delivered suggests the strongest stimulation arises in the most posterior regions of IPS (IPS1 and IPS24); however, auditory spatial attention relies primarily on higher IPS regions (Michalka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the current flow modeling and a citation to prior research on IPS regions involved in auditory attention.

claim: External stimulation can cause neural entrainment, synchronizing intrinsic oscillations to the external input.
source: Some past studies suggest that stimulation can cause neural entrainment, synchronizing intrinsic oscillations to the external input (e.g., see Helfrich et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: External stimulation has been shown to modulate the spontaneous activity of neurons by shifting resting cell membrane potentials, directly influencing endogenous brain oscillations.
source: External stimulation also has been shown to modulate the spontaneous activity of neurons by shifting resting cell membrane potentials (Purpura and Mcmurtry, 1965; Nitsche et al., 2003), directly influencing endogenous brain oscillations (Bergmann et al., 2009; Zaehle et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the current study, the effects of HD-tACS did not persist into post-stimulation testing.
source: In our study, the effects of HD-tACS did not persist into post-stimulation testing (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: More intense stimulation may elicit an after-effect of tACS.
source: It may be that more intense stimulation would elicit an after-effect (Moliadze et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about why no after-effects were observed, supported by a citation.

claim: Alpha stimulation effects may be more prominent and after-effects more long-lasting when the exact frequency of stimulation is matched to the individual subject's natural peak alpha frequency.
source: Alternatively, alpha stimulation effects may be more prominent and after-effects more long-lasting when the exact frequency of stimulation is matched to the individual subject's natural peak alpha frequency (Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about factors that might enhance stimulation effects, supported by a citation.

claim: When the driving frequency of tACS stimulation matches the intrinsic oscillation frequency of a particular neural assembly, stimulation will be more effective at entraining relevant neural responses.
source: It may be that when the driving frequency of tACS stimulation matches the intrinsic oscillation frequency of a particular neural assembly (such as the assembly responsible for intrinsic parietal alpha oscillations), stimulation will be more effective at entraining relevant neural responses.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of tACS effectiveness.

claim: Matching the tACS stimulation to an individual's measured parietal alpha oscillations may preferentially influence the relevant parietal neural population involved in steering spatial attention.
source: If so, matching the tACS stimulation to an individual's measured parietal alpha oscillations may preferentially influence the relevant parietal neural population involved in steering spatial attention.
evidence: This is speculation about how to improve stimulation effectiveness.

claim: Closed-loop methods that individually match the frequency of HD-tACS to endogenous neural oscillations in real-time may provide more robust changes in brain function.
source: Closed-loop methods that individually match the frequency of HD-tACS to endogenous neural oscillations in real-time thus may provide more robust changes in brain function.
evidence: This is speculation about future methodological improvements.

claim: Abnormalities in parietal alpha and its distribution across cerebral hemispheres have been documented in numerous disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease, depression and ADHD).
source: Abnormalities in parietal alpha and its distribution across cerebral hemispheres have been documented in numerous disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease [Koelewijn et al., 2017], depression [Bruder et al., 1997] and ADHD [Hale et al., 2009]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on clinical populations.

claim: Studies that directly manipulate oscillatory parietal activity lay critical groundwork for development of interventions to alleviate problems due to atypical cortical mechanisms in a range of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Studies like ours, which directly manipulate oscillatory parietal activity, lay critical groundwork for development of interventions to alleviate problems due to atypical cortical mechanisms in a range of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential clinical applications of this research.

claim: Thirty-eight volunteers gave written consent to procedures approved by the Boston University Institutional Review Board.
source: Thirty-eight volunteers gave written consent to procedures approved by the Boston University Institutional Review Board.
evidence: This is a statement about the study procedures and ethics approval.

claim: Twenty volunteers aged between 18–24 years (mean 21.15 year., standard deviation 3.01 year.; 13 females, seven males) participated in the main experiment.
source: Twenty volunteers aged between 18–24 years (mean 21.15 year., standard deviation 3.01 year.; 13 females, seven males) participated in the main experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Eighteen volunteers aged between 18–24 years (mean 22.11 year., standard deviation 2.4 year.; 15 females, three males) participated in the control experiment.
source: Eighteen volunteers aged between 18–24 years (mean 22.11 year., standard deviation 2.4 year.; 15 females, three males) participated in the control experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All participants had clinically normal audiometric thresholds in both ears for frequencies from 250 Hz to 8 k Hz (thresholds less than 20 dB HL).
source: All participants had clinically normal audiometric thresholds in both ears for frequencies from 250 Hz to 8 k Hz (thresholds less than 20 dB HL).
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for study participants.

claim: A pilot experiment with six subjects was conducted to estimate effect size, and based on this, 14 subjects were estimated to be needed to achieve a power of 0.903.
source: We conducted a pilot experiment with six subjects and estimated effect size for the 'attend left, continuous, spatial attention' trials during alpha stimulation of right parietal cortex. Given that we also planned on testing 'attend right, continuous, spatial attention' trials, we estimated that we needed 14 subjects to achieve a power of 0.903 (correcting the family-wise error rate for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a description of the power analysis conducted to determine sample size.

claim: Because some attrition was anticipated, 20 subjects were recruited in the main experiment and 18 in the control experiment, all of whom completed the experiments.
source: Because we anticipated some attrition, we recruited 20 subjects in the main experiment and 18 in the control experiment, all of whom completed the experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the recruitment strategy and completion rate.

claim: In each trial, sound stimuli comprised two competing speech streams: a target and a distractor, both five syllables long.
source: In each trial, sound stimuli comprised two competing speech streams: a target and a distractor. Both target and distractor streams were five syllables long.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The syllables were chosen from the same set of voiced-stop-consonant-vowel utterances (/ba/,/da/, and/ga/; each 388 ms in duration) recorded by one female talker and one male talker (F0 roughly 189 Hz and 125 Hz, respectively).
source: The syllables were chosen from the same set of voiced-stop-consonant-vowel utterances (/ba/,/da/, and/ga/; each 388 ms in duration) recorded by one female talker and one male talker (F0 roughly 189 Hz and 125 Hz, respectively, as estimated by Praat software).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each syllable was spatialized to be perceived as either 90 degrees to the left or 90 degrees to the right by convolving raw recordings with manikin head-related transfer functions.
source: Each syllable was spatialized to be perceived as either 90 degrees to the left or 90 degrees to the right by convolving raw recordings with manikin head-related transfer functions (Gardner and Martin, 1995).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus spatialization method.

claim: Both the target stream and the distractor stream were isochronous, with an inter-syllable interval of 433 ms, but the two streams were temporally interdigitated with the distractor stream beginning 180 ms before the target stream.
source: Both the target stream and the distractor stream were isochronous, with an inter-syllable interval of 433 ms. However, the two streams were temporally interdigitated: the distractor stream always began first, 180 ms before the target stream.
evidence: This is a description of the temporal structure of the stimuli.

claim: On each trial, the listener's goal was to count the number of/ga/ syllables in the target stream.
source: On each trial, the listener's goal was to count the number of/ga/ syllables in the target stream
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: Stimuli were presented via earphones (ER-2, Etymotic Research, Inc) in a double-walled Eckel sound-treated booth at Boston University at a sound pressure level of approximately 75 dB.
source: Stimuli were presented via earphones (ER-2, Etymotic Research, Inc) in a double-walled Eckel sound-treated booth at Boston University. All sound stimuli were presented at a sound pressure level of approximately 75 dB.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus presentation setup.

claim: In the main experiment, the two testing days were separated by 1–14 days (mean of 2.45 days; standard deviation of 3.12 days).
source: In the main experiment, the two testing days were separated by 1–14 days (mean of 2.45 days; standard deviation of 3.12 days).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline.

claim: In the control experiment, the two testing days were separated by 1–16 days (mean of 4.61 days; standard deviation of 5.04 days).
source: In the control experiment, the two testing days were separated by 1–16 days (mean of 4.61 days; standard deviation of 5.04 days).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline.

claim: HD-tACS was administered using the Soterix M × N-9 High Definition-Transcranial Electrical Current (HD-tES) Stimulator (Model 9002A, Soterix Medical, New York, NY).
source: HD-tACS was administered using the Soterix M × N-9 High Definition-Transcranial Electrical Current (HD-tES) Stimulator (Model 9002A, Soterix Medical, New York, NY).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulation equipment.

claim: To target right IPS, an electrode montage was created based on a current-flow model generated by the Soterix HD-Explore software (version 4.1, Soterix Medical, New York, NY).
source: To target right IPS, an electrode montage was created based on a current-flow model generated by the Soterix HD-Explore software (version 4.1, Soterix Medical, New York, NY).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulation targeting method.

claim: The major stimulating electrode was placed at P2 with a stimulation intensity of 1.5mA, and four return electrodes were placed at CP2 (−0.6mA), P4 (−0.225mA), Pz (−0.075mA), and PO4 (−0.6mA).
source: The major stimulating electrode was placed at P2 with a stimulation intensity of 1.5mA, and four return electrodes were placed at CP2 (−0.6mA), P4 (−0.225mA), Pz (−0.075mA), and PO4 (−0.6mA).
evidence: This is a description of the electrode montage.

claim: Both Stimulation and Sham sessions delivered a bipolar sinusoidal waveform at 10 Hz in the main experiment.
source: Both Stimulation and Sham sessions delivered a bipolar sinusoidal waveform at 10 Hz (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulation waveform, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A 10 Hz stimulation rate was chosen for the main experiment, which is close to the peak reported for most subjects (in the 10–11 Hz range).
source: When targeting parietal alpha oscillations in the main experiment, we chose a 10 Hz stimulation rate, which is close to the peak reported for most subjects (in the 10–11 Hz range).
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the stimulation frequency choice.

claim: The control experiment used a 6 Hz rate, which is the median peak theta frequency.
source: The control experiment used a 6 Hz rate, which is the median peak theta frequency (Jacobs, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the control experiment stimulation frequency, supported by a citation.

claim: The total current delivered was 1.5 mA at maximum.
source: The total current delivered was 1.5 mA at maximum.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulation intensity.

claim: Previous tACS studies have commonly used 1.5–2 mA stimulation intensity.
source: While the most effective intensity and duration for HD-tACS or traditional tACS stimulation is not known, previous tACS studies have commonly used 1.5–2 mA (Helfrich et al., 2014; Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019; Klaus and Schutter, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A relatively conservative and widely used stimulation intensity of 1.5 mA was chosen to mitigate any adverse effect of stimulation.
source: With very few studies to reference on the effectiveness of HD-tACS intensity, we arbitrarily chose a relatively conservative and widely used stimulation intensity of 1.5 mA to mitigate any adverse effect of stimulation (Matsumoto and Ugawa, 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the stimulation intensity choice.

claim: In the HD-tACS session, stimulation ramped up to 1.5 mA over 30 s at the beginning of the 20 min stimulation block, and ramped down over 30 s at the end, yielding 19 min of continuous 1.5 mA stimulation during the middle of the block.
source: In the HD-tACS session, stimulation ramped up to 1.5 mA over 30 s at the beginning of the 20 min stimulation block, and ramped down over 30 s at the end, yielding 19 min of continuous 1.5 mA stimulation during the middle of the block.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulation protocol.

claim: During the middle block of the Sham session, stimulation ramped up to 1.5 mA over 30 s and then immediately ramped down to 0 mA in the following 30 s; in the final minute of the block, stimulation ramped up and then down.
source: During the middle block of the Sham session, stimulation ramped up to 1.5 mA over 30 s and then immediately ramped down to 0 mA in the following 30 s; in the final minute of the block, stimulation ramped up and then down.
evidence: This is a description of the sham stimulation protocol.

claim: In pilot experiments, subjects were asked verbally whether they could differentiate sham and stimulation sessions, and none could.
source: In our pilot experiments, we asked subjects verbally whether they could differentiate sham and stimulation sessions. None could.
evidence: This is a description of the blinding effectiveness from pilot data.

claim: In past HD-tACS studies using comparable stimulation parameters, subjects' ability to differentiate sham from stimulation was systematically probed, and in no case were responses significantly different from random guessing.
source: This confirmed the experience we have from our past HD-tACS studies using comparable stimulation parameters (including intensity, duration, sink-source electrode configuration, low frequencies), where we systematically probed the subjects' ability to differentiate sham from stimulation; in no case were responses significantly different from random guessing (Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019; Reinhart, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: Alpha frequency stimulation has been reported to be more effective in darkness.
source: Because alpha frequency stimulation has been reported to be more effective in darkness (Kanai et al., 2008), all subjects but one performed the experiment in the dark
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All subjects but one performed the experiment in the dark; the exception reported suffering from claustrophobia and performed the task in typical lighting.
source: all subjects but one performed the experiment in the dark; the exception reported suffering from claustrophobia and performed the task in typical lighting.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.
